disclaimer: Education, not financial advice. Outcomes as of 2026.

scenes.headline: 10 times government bonds weren't risk-free
scenes.body: Greece. Argentina. Sri Lanka. Ghana. And one story from South Africa.
scenes.voiceover: You've probably heard that lending to the government is risk-free. Here are ten times it wasn't, and what risk-free really means for your money.

scenes.headline: From far away to close to your rand bond
scenes.body: Foreign-currency debt → couldn't print its own money → local-currency debt.
scenes.voiceover: We've ranked them not by size, but by how close they come to a South African holding a government bond in rands. First, governments that borrowed in someone else's currency. Then one that couldn't print its own money. Then the ones that hit bonds in their own currency.

scenes.headline: Zambia, 2020
scenes.voiceover: Number ten. Zambia, 2020.

scenes.headline: Missed a $42.5 million bond payment
scenes.voiceover: In November twenty twenty, Zambia missed a payment of about forty-two and a half million dollars on its dollar bonds. It became the first African government to default in the COVID era.
scenes.name: Zambia, 2020
scenes.body: The first African government to default in the COVID era.

scenes.headline: Restructured, after almost four years of talks
scenes.voiceover: It wasn't a lot of money. The problem was what it signalled: the debt was too big to keep paying. Bondholders accepted new terms in twenty twenty-four, after almost four years of negotiation.
scenes.name: Zambia, 2020

scenes.headline: Ecuador, 2008
scenes.voiceover: Number nine. Ecuador, 2008.

scenes.headline: Refused to pay $3.2 billion of bonds
scenes.voiceover: In twenty oh eight, Ecuador's government stopped paying three point two billion dollars of bonds, not because it couldn't, but because it called the debt illegitimate. Then it offered to buy the bonds back at about thirty-five cents per dollar.
scenes.name: Ecuador, 2008
scenes.body: The government called the debt illegitimate, then offered about 35 cents per dollar.

scenes.headline: Ukraine, 2015
scenes.voiceover: Number eight. Ukraine, 2015.

scenes.eyebrow: October 2015, after the war in the east began
scenes.headline: Bondholders accepted a restructuring
scenes.voiceover: In twenty fifteen, after conflict broke out in its east and its economy shrank, Ukraine restructured about thirteen point three billion dollars of debt. War is one of the oldest reasons governments stop paying on time.
scenes.name: Ukraine, 2015

scenes.headline: Venezuela, 2017
scenes.voiceover: Number seven. Venezuela, 2017.

scenes.headline: An oil giant that ran out of dollars
scenes.voiceover: Venezuela has some of the world's largest oil reserves. But when oil prices fell and production collapsed, it ran out of the dollars it needed. In twenty seventeen it defaulted on about thirty-one billion dollars of debt.
scenes.name: Venezuela, 2017

scenes.headline: One of the longest-running defaults of recent years
scenes.voiceover: It became one of the longest-running defaults of recent years.

scenes.headline: Lebanon, 2020
scenes.voiceover: Number six. Lebanon, 2020.

scenes.headline: Then the banks froze people's savings
scenes.voiceover: Lebanon had never defaulted. Then in March twenty twenty, it missed a one point two billion dollar bond payment, and about thirty-one billion dollars went into default. Its banks, which held much of that debt, restricted people's access to their own savings.
scenes.name: Lebanon, 2020

scenes.headline: Sri Lanka, 2022
scenes.voiceover: Number five. Sri Lanka, 2022.

scenes.headline: Suspended about $51 billion of foreign debt
scenes.voiceover: In April twenty twenty-two, Sri Lanka ran so low on dollars it couldn't import enough fuel or medicine. It suspended payments on about fifty-one billion dollars of foreign debt. Inflation hit almost seventy percent, and the president fled the country.
scenes.name: Sri Lanka, 2022
scenes.body: Inflation hit 69.8% in September 2022. The rupee lost about 80% of its value.

scenes.headline: Mostly restructured, with an IMF programme
scenes.voiceover: As of twenty twenty-six, most of that debt has been restructured, under an IMF programme.
scenes.name: Sri Lanka, 2022

scenes.headline: Argentina, 2001
scenes.voiceover: Number four. Argentina, 2001.

scenes.headline: The record default of its time
scenes.voiceover: Argentina had tied its peso one to one with the US dollar, and borrowed heavily in dollars. In December two thousand and one, it defaulted on about eighty-two billion dollars, the biggest default of its time.
scenes.name: Argentina, 2001

scenes.headline: Bank deposits frozen. Unemployment near 25%.
scenes.voiceover: Banks froze people's deposits. The economy shrank by about eleven percent in a year. And Argentina has defaulted nine times since independence.

scenes.headline: Greece, 2012
scenes.voiceover: Number three. Greece, 2012.

scenes.headline: Bondholders accepted a 53.5% cut to face value
scenes.voiceover: Greece borrowed in euros, a currency it couldn't print. In March twenty twelve, private bondholders accepted a fifty-three point five percent cut to the face value of their bonds, the largest debt restructuring in history.
scenes.name: Greece, 2012

stat.label: Cut to the face value of private bondholders' Greek bonds

scenes.headline: Greece dwarfs every other default
scenes.voiceover: Measured by the debt involved, about two hundred and sixty-four billion dollars, nothing else comes close. And here's the detail that matters for us: most of those bonds were issued under Greek law, and Greece changed its own law to make all holders accept the deal.

scenes.headline: Russia, 1998
scenes.voiceover: Number two. Russia, 1998.

scenes.headline: Defaulted on bonds in its own currency
scenes.voiceover: Here's the one that breaks a common belief: that a government can always pay debt in its own currency, because it can print it. In August nineteen ninety-eight, Russia defaulted on its own ruble bonds, and the ruble lost about three quarters of its value.
scenes.name: Russia, 1998
scenes.body: Short-term ruble bonds called GKOs. The ruble then lost about three quarters of its value.

scenes.headline: Willing to pay, but blocked by sanctions
scenes.voiceover: And in twenty twenty-two, Russia was ruled in default for a different reason: it had the money, but sanctions blocked the payments. Risk isn't only about money.
scenes.name: Russia, 1998

scenes.headline: South Africa's debt standstill
scenes.body: About $13.6 billion of mostly bank and private-sector short-term foreign debt (SARB).
scenes.voiceover: Before number one, a story from closer to home. In August nineteen eighty-five, after P W Botha's Rubicon speech, foreign banks refused to roll over South Africa's short-term loans. The country declared a standstill on repaying about thirteen point six billion dollars of foreign debt, mostly owed by banks and companies.

scenes.headline: Fully repaid in 2001, 16 years to the day
scenes.body: Historians disagree on whether it counts as a sovereign default.
scenes.voiceover: Historians still disagree on whether it counts as a sovereign default. The last payment was made in August two thousand and one, sixteen years to the day after the speech.

scenes.eyebrow: Its own currency, its own savers
scenes.headline: Ghana, 2022
scenes.voiceover: Number one. Ghana, 2022.

scenes.headline: Local bonds held by local institutions were restructured too
scenes.voiceover: And number one. In December twenty twenty-two, Ghana suspended payments on about thirteen billion dollars of foreign bonds. But it also exchanged more than eleven billion dollars' worth of its own local-currency bonds, held largely by local banks, pension funds and insurers, for new bonds that paid less and later.
scenes.name: Ghana, 2022
scenes.body: More than $11bn of cedi bonds, held largely by banks, pension funds and insurers.

scenes.headline: It happened at home, in the local currency
scenes.voiceover: That's why it's number one for us. It's close to home, it's recent, and it hit local savers' institutions in the local currency. As of twenty twenty-six, Ghana has restructured its bonds and is paying again.
scenes.name: Ghana, 2022

scenes.headline: Low credit risk. Not zero risk. Not inflation-proof.
scenes.body: Credit risk: will you be paid back? Inflation risk: will the money still buy as much?
scenes.voiceover: So what does risk-free really mean? Usually, low credit risk: the government is very likely to pay you back. It doesn't mean zero risk, and it doesn't mean your money keeps its value. Weimar Germany and Zimbabwe paid people back in money that had become worthless.

scenes.headline: RSA Retail Savings Bonds: lower credit risk, not none
scenes.body: About 90% of SA government debt is in rand. Fixed-rate bonds carry more inflation risk; inflation-linked bonds are designed to reduce it.
scenes.voiceover: About ninety percent of South Africa's government debt is in rands, so RSA Retail Savings Bonds carry lower credit risk, but not none. They come in fixed-rate and inflation-linked types. Fixed-rate bonds carry more inflation risk. Inflation-linked bonds are designed to reduce it. This is education, not financial advice.

scenes.headline: Did you know government bonds could fail?
scenes.voiceover: Did you know government bonds could fail? Tell us in the comments.

endcard.title: Know your risk
endcard.subtitle: Subscribe for South African money, explained.

They say lending to the government is risk-free. Here are 10 times it wasn't, from Zambia and Argentina to Greece, Russia and Ghana, plus South Africa's 1985 debt standstill, and what 'risk-free' really means for your money.

Ranking: by how close each case comes to a South African holding a rand government bond (foreign-currency debt, then a country that couldn't print its own money, then local-currency debt).
